title: Applying Additive Schema Migrations
learningObjectives: Identify additive schema changes and explain their compatibility benefits.
Add a column with an appropriate default in SQLite.
Group schema, backfill and history updates in a transaction.
Verify the new schema field and backfilled values.

understand.concept: An additive migration introduces a compatible schema element such as a nullable column, a column with a safe default or a new index. Additive changes can support rolling application deployments when old and new application versions can both work with the schema.
understand.whyItMatters: Small, compatible changes reduce deployment risk and allow applications to transition gradually.
understand.analogy: A migration is like a numbered building renovation plan: each change has a recorded step, a verification and a recovery plan.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model transactional DDL, locking, data backfills, version checks or application compatibility.

explain.narrative:
## Additive changes
Adding a nullable column or a column with an appropriate default is often safer than renaming or dropping a column immediately. Create new structures before deploying application code that depends on them.

## Migration transaction
Where the engine supports transactional DDL, wrap related schema and data changes in one transaction. Record the migration version only after the change succeeds.

## Expand and contract
A common rollout pattern is to add a new column, deploy code that writes both old and new fields, backfill existing rows, switch reads, and only later remove the old field after all application versions stop using it.

examples.title: Create a version-one products table
examples.code: CREATE TABLE mig18_products (product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_name TEXT NOT NULL);
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates create a version-one products table in SQLite. Verify the migration state before and after the operation.

examples.title: Insert existing products
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates insert existing products in SQLite. Verify the migration state before and after the operation.

examples.title: Create migration history
examples.code: CREATE TABLE mig18_product_history (version INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, description TEXT NOT NULL); INSERT INTO mig18_product_history VALUES (1, 'Create products');
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates create migration history in SQLite. Verify the migration state before and after the operation.

examples.title: Apply an additive category column and record version two
examples.code: BEGIN; ALTER TABLE mig18_products ADD COLUMN category TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'general'; UPDATE mig18_products SET category = 'stationery'; INSERT INTO mig18_product_history VALUES (2, 'Add product category'); COMMIT;
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates apply an additive category column and record version two in SQLite. Verify the migration state before and after the operation.

examples.title: Verify the new column and values
examples.code: SELECT product_name, category FROM mig18_products ORDER BY product_id;
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates verify the new column and values in SQLite. Verify the migration state before and after the operation.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples and inspect the new category column for existing product rows.
practise.independentTask: Plan an additive migration that adds a nullable contact field, backfills known values and records a new schema version. Explain how old and new application versions can coexist during rollout.
hints: Add the new structure before relying on it in application code.
Choose a safe default or nullable definition for existing rows.
Use a transaction when the engine supports transactional DDL.
Record the migration version only after successful changes.
Verify existing rows as well as new writes.

options: A change that adds compatible schema elements without immediately removing existing ones
A command that deletes all old columns
A database backup
A query that returns no rows
questions.answer: A change that adds compatible schema elements without immediately removing existing ones
questions.explanation: Additive migrations introduce new structures while preserving existing ones.

questions.prompt: Why add a column before removing an old one?
options: It can allow old and new application versions to coexist during rollout
It forces every application to stop
It removes the need for testing
It disables constraints
questions.answer: It can allow old and new application versions to coexist during rollout
questions.explanation: Expand-and-contract reduces compatibility risk during deployment.

questions.prompt: When should the migration version be recorded?
options: After the schema and data changes succeed
Before any SQL is executed
Only after a user logs out
Before the backup is taken
questions.answer: After the schema and data changes succeed
questions.explanation: The history should reflect successfully applied changes.

options: Populates a newly introduced field for existing rows
Drops an index
Creates a new database user
Renames the primary key
questions.answer: Populates a newly introduced field for existing rows
questions.explanation: A backfill updates existing records to satisfy the new data model.

questions.prompt: What should be checked after adding a column?
options: Existing and new rows have the intended values
Only the column's visual width
The database filename
The SQL editor theme
questions.answer: Existing and new rows have the intended values
questions.explanation: Post-migration checks must verify both schema and data.
